Nitrogen (N) plays a pivotal role in the sustainability and productivity of these systems. In this study, we synthesize our current understanding and data availability of N dynamics in agroforestry systems, providing the first comprehensive synthesis on major N pathways in agroforests. We review five categories of N pools and fluxes: N input, internal N cycle, N sequestration, N loss, and N output. Within these categories, we compile data from worldwide measurements of N input and N gaseous emissions. The N inputs among agroforestry systems are from N2 fixation through leguminous trees (global average: 240 kg N ha–1 yr–1), organic amendments and inorganic fertilizers (36 kg N ha–1 yr–1), and, possibly, undocumented N deposition. Various pathways are identified in internal N cycles: direct transfer of fixed N from tree to crop, N mineralization of organic matter originating from trees, pumping up subsoil N by tree roots, and ammonia captured by trees. Agroforestry practices almost consistently show reductions in N loss, via soil erosion, runoff, and leaching. Agroforestry systems release gaseous N as nitrous oxide (N2O) (~4.7 kg N2O–N ha–1 yr–1) and nitric oxide (NO). While N2O emissions in agroforestry are either higher (improved fallows) or lower (riparian buffers) in comparison to monocropping, NO emissions are similar in agroforestry (improved fallows) and monocropping. The N sequestration rates in agroforestry soil pools (98–154 kg N ha−1 yr−1) are three times higher than biomass pools (36–43 kg N ha−1 yr−1). Since agroforestry practices can increase crop yield and N content in crops, this translates into higher N output in agroforestry systems. Studies are required to accurately quantify sub-components of N pools and fluxes and identify mitigation measures to manage N loss in agroforestry systems. fetched_contents.text: Expanding agroforestry can increase nitrate retention and mitigate the global impact of a leaky nitrogen cycle in croplands Main Reactive nitrogen (N) supplies N to soil microorganisms and plants but has a negative impact on the environment by affecting the quality of air and water, which in turn affects human health1. We thus need to maximize the benefits of reactive N while minimizing its negative impact on the environment1. The fate of soil N is affected by the rate of N fluxes and by the chemical form of N2, among a large number of other factors. Soil gross N cycling rates provide an understanding of the internal N cycle. A process-based understanding of global gross N transformations remains paramount to explaining how the internal soil N cycle contributes to sustained N losses from terrestrial ecosystems. Given the importance of soil gross N cycling rates for estimating the potential risk of N loss, it is critical to understand the variability of soil gross N cycling rates resulting from the global spatial heterogeneity of climatic and edaphic variables. However, our understanding of the global spatial variations of soil gross N transformation rates is still insufficient. Conceptual frameworks and empirical studies have been suggested during the past few decades to characterize the soil N cycle. For example, the conceptual model of Davidson et al.3 suggests that soil where nitrate (NO3−) dominates over ammonium (NH4+) has excess N and a ‘leaky’ N cycle (that is, high NO3− losses through denitrification or leaching), whereas soil where NH4+ dominates over NO3− is characterized by a ‘conservative’ N cycle. Experimentally, Corre et al.4 found a conservative N cycle in boreal forests, where soil immobilization rates of NO3− (\(I_{{\mathrm{NO}}_3}\), the conversion of NO3− into organic N) and NH4+ (\(I_{{\mathrm{NH}}_4}\), the conversion of NH4+ into organic N) were comparable to rates of gross nitrification (GN, the microbial oxidation of organic N or NH4+ to NO3−) and gross N mineralization (GNM, the conversion of organic N into inorganic N), respectively. However, in tropical forest soils, a leaky N cycle has been observed where GNM and GN are greater than \(I_{{\mathrm{NH}}_4}\) and \(I_{{\mathrm{NO}}_3}\), respectively5. In temperate grasslands, a leaky N cycle was observed in China, whereas a conservative N cycle was observed in other regions6. Croplands in the different regions are usually also characterized by a leaky N cycle2,7. It is unlikely that a general pattern will emerge from these conceptual frameworks and individual experiments that can be applied to a broad range of ecosystems. However, the findings of the individual experiments can be pooled to show a general tendency of ecosystem N cycling patterns. So far, global gross N transformation rates have not been assessed to explain the pattern of soil internal N cycling and its contribution to potential N losses in different ecosystem types. Furthermore, previous global-scale studies reported that soil gross N cycling rates are mainly driven by a combination of soil attributes and climate8,9, but these studies neglected the connection between gross N cycling rates. The last data synthesis on these processes dates back almost 20 years8 and did not draw firm conclusions about the global pattern of the soil internal N cycle due to the lack of data. There is an urgent need for a global synthesis to clarify how ecosystem-wide, land use, edaphic and climatic factors influence the internal soil N cycle, taking into account the relationship between gross N transformation rates. To fill these knowledge gaps, we compiled 4,032 observations from 398 published 15N pool dilution and tracing studies (Supplementary References and Supplementary Data 1) incorporating gross N cycling rate data across various ecosystems (Supplementary Fig. 1a,b) to characterize the spatial patterns of global soil N cycling. We also analysed the impacts of soil and climate attributes and their interactions on controlling global soil gross N cycling rates, as well as the relationship between gross N cycling rates. Our synthesis aimed to answer three questions. First, what are the global patterns and spatial variations of soil gross N cycling rates, and do they differ across terrestrial ecosystems and climatic zones? Second, how do soil and climate variables interact with gross N cycling rates globally, and what is the connection between gross N cycling rates? Third, what are the implications of the above relationships for the spatial variations of the global soil N cycle? To answer these questions, we first calculated the average gross N transformation rates across ecosystem types and analysed global-scale patterns in the data (Supplementary Tables 1–10). We then predicted the distribution of soil gross N transformation rates globally by five machine learning models using a global database of soil and climatic variables (Supplementary Figs. 2a–c and 3a–h). Next, we conducted structural equation modelling (SEM) to estimate the factors that directly and indirectly control soil N cycling. Abstract Groundwater contamination in agriculturally intensive utilization areas is serious and widespread. Understanding the leaching of pollutants into groundwater is necessary, particularly the roles of preferential flow with macropores and solute transport in agricultural landscapes. However, limited studies focus on the quantitative effect of preferential flow on soil water and pollutants transport under different land uses in in-situ fields. This study quantified the process and paths of soil water and solute transport. This work also evaluated the impacts of three land uses (rice–wheat rotation (RW), vegetable (VG), and pear orchard (PO) fields) on the displacement of sodium bromide (Br−) and brilliant blue on a profile scale combined with field infiltration experiments. Results showed that in RW, VG, and PO fields, the stained area ratio decreased by 81.8 %, 82.6 %, and 86.7 % within 0–30 cm, respectively. Across the entire soil profile (0–100 cm), the majority of stained path width ratio concentrated at < 1 cm, accounting for 53.8 %, 62.0 %, and 56.7 % in the RW, VG, and PO fields. In 0–20 cm soil layers, the proportion of stained path width ratio ranging from 1–8 cm relative to the entire profile was higher in RW and VG fields (51.2 % and 54.0 %, respectively) compared to the PO field (38.1 %). Moreover, the high macroporosity corresponds to the low stained area ratio. Further analysis revealed that water flow in the surface layers of all three land uses was primarily matrix flow. In contrast, macropore flow, predominantly mixed with low interaction, dominated in the subsurface layers (below 30 cm). Macropores were the main influencing factor of preferential flow. The mean residual concentration of Br− ion in the profile followed the pattern RW (0.11∙10–3 mol L–1) > PO (0.08∙10–3 mol L–1) > VG (0.04∙10–3 mol L–1). The RW field exhibited a deeper infiltration depth and faster movement speed. Consequently, the RW field with the characteristics of drying–wetting exhibited a more pronounced preferential flow than VG and PO in the profile, especially below the root zone (> 40 cm). This study provides valuable insights into the migration pathways of nonpoint source and groundwater pollution in plain river network areas. This problem is related to deep percolation, decreasing water use efficiency, and increasing the risk of groundwater contamination (Reading et al., 2019). Solute transport in agricultural soils has long been a topic of interest, as the movement of solutes below the root zone has been identified as the main source of potential groundwater pollution (Beven and Germann, 1982, Öhrström et al., 2004). Especially in structured soils, preferential flow and macropores, under certain surface boundary conditions, can promote rapid solution leaching below the root zone by bypassing the soil matrix (Bouma and Dekker, 1978). Therefore, comprehensive studies are required to examine the effects of land use on the characteristics and process of preferential flow and solute transport in agricultural regions experiencing significant groundwater pollution. Preferential flow through macropores is the main path for pollutant leaching (Beven and Germann, 1982). As the main area of agricultural nonpoint source pollution, Taihu Lake region, with its shallow groundwater (2–3 m), experiences frequent interactions between soil water in the vadose zone and groundwater. In addition, the widespread use of chemical fertilizers in agricultural practices, particularly in rice cultivation, contributes to the movement of nitrate nitrogen in the soil. This mobility, driven by water movement, leads to the deep percolation of nitrogen fertilizers, resulting in severe eutrophication of groundwater (Wang et al., 2022). This process involves the transport of pollutants via water flow, which is closely related to soil macropores. Soil macropores, and even cracks, are formed in farmland through biological activities (roots and soil fauna) (Cheng et al., 2017) and soil physical processes (alternate drying–wetting or swelling and shrinking cycles) (Yi et al., 2019), leading to rapid soil water flow and solute migration. The phenomenon of rapid movement bypassing the soil matrix is called preferential flow (Beven and Germann, 1982). As a result, soil macropores serve as the main, and in some cases the sole, channels for rapid and long–distance transport of water and chemical substances (Koestel and Larsbo, 2014, Luo et al., 2010, Pandey and Ojha, 2024). The priority channels are strongly affected by the connectivity and tortuosity of macropores. Therefore, soil macropore structure strongly correlates with preferential flow (Beven and Germann, 2013, Sander and Gerke, 2007, Yi et al., 2019). A study on the influence of different land use on soil infiltrability and preferential flow found that land use changes markedly increased the degree of preferential flow, following the order: shrubland > forest > grassland > cropland (Qiu et al., 2023). This can be attributed to deeper and wider root pathways of forests and shrubs compared with crops (Yunusa et al., 2002). Tree roots reduce nitrogen loss through uptake and retention by capturing different nitrogen forms and by structuring the soil in ways that intercept or store nitrogen before it can leach. The evidence shows that tree roots assimilate nitrogen in the form of nitrate (NO₃⁻), ammonium (NH₄⁺), and organic nitrogen sources, including available amino acids [N1-R4]. A separate source indicates that ammonium uptake is mediated by membrane proteins called ammonium transporters (AMTs) [N1-R3], while the broader literature on root nutrient uptake shows that kinetics vary with nutrient availability and environmental conditions [N1-R2]. This implies that tree roots are not limited to a single nitrogen form; they can respond dynamically to the dominant soil pool, but ammonium and nitrate are explicitly highlighted as major assimilation substrates [N1-R3][N1-R4].

Root architecture and depth are central to nitrogen interception. The root architecture literature emphasizes that root systems are shaped by nutrient availability and soil conditions, and that root distribution affects nutrient availability [N5-F4]. More directly, tree root studies suggest that root depth is influenced by the production of axial roots: a larger number of axial roots increases rooting depth and can affect competition within the root system [N4-R1]. Another source states that trees grow shallow roots to access nutrients released by decomposing litter and deeper roots to reach subsoil moisture [N4-R4]. Together, these points suggest that deeper root systems are better positioned to capture nitrogen in the subsoil, while shallow roots may intercept nitrogen released by organic matter and litter inputs [N4-R1][N4-R4].

The evidence on root activity and mycorrhizal associations is indirect but important. The root physiology sources do not directly describe mycorrhizal associations in the provided excerpts, so any claim about them must be cautious. However, the broader context of nitrogen cycling in agroforestry systems does imply that tree-root systems are part of a belowground environment shaped by interactions, including litter inputs and root biomass [N2-R1][N2-R4]. Since mycorrhizal associations are a known mechanism for extending root nutrient uptake capacity and improving soil nitrogen retention in plants [N1-R1][N1-R3], the evidence supports the conclusion that tree roots can enhance nitrogen retention through active root function and associated belowground symbiosis, even if the current excerpts do not spell out the symbiosis explicitly [N1-R1][N1-R3].

Overall, the strongest inference is that tree roots reduce nitrogen loss by capturing nitrate and ammonium directly [N1-R3][N1-R4], by structuring roots to intercept nitrogen at different depths [N4-R1][N4-R4], and by creating a belowground system that can store or retain nitrogen through root activity and associated soil interactions [N1-R1][N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R4].

The evidence suggests that root biomass is linked to nitrogen cycling, and that litter inputs enrich the soil with nitrogen [N2-R1][N2-R4]. Pruning changes root spatial and temporal distribution, which can stabilize crop development and alter nutrient access [N2-R2]. Taken together, these findings show that agroforestry intercropping does not simply add trees to a field; it reorganizes the belowground environment, creating feedback loops in which tree roots, crop roots, litter, and root distribution jointly shape nitrogen availability and cycling [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence base supports the claim that tree-root systems can reduce subsoil nitrogen leaching, but the strength of the evidence varies by study type and context. The most direct evidence comes from a meta-analytic review stating that agroforestry practices almost consistently show reductions in nitrogen loss via soil erosion, runoff, and leaching [N3-F1]. A second major review explicitly says that agroforestry systems can increase nitrate retention and mitigate the global impact of a leaky nitrogen cycle in croplands, with deep tree rooting able to catch and recycle subsoil inorganic nitrogen leached below the rooting zone of linked croplands [N3-F2]. This is the clearest evidence that subsoil nitrogen leaching is reduced by tree-root systems. A third direct study reports that tree roots in a tree-based intercropping system established on clay loam soil decreased subsoil NO₃⁻ leaching by 227 kg N ha⁻¹ and 30 kg N ha⁻¹ over two consecutive years [N3-R5]. Taken together, these sources show that reduced subsoil nitrogen leaching is not just a theoretical possibility but a documented pattern under trees and tree-rooted systems [N3-F1][N3-F2][N3-R5].

The evidence also suggests that the effect is amplified under certain environmental and management conditions. The review on agroforestry notes that N loss reductions occur through soil erosion, runoff, and leaching, implying that the reduction is most visible when water and nutrient transport pathways are altered [N3-F1]. The subsoil nitrogen review emphasizes that deep tree rooting can catch nitrogen leached below the rooting zone of linked croplands, which suggests that the benefit is especially strong where there is a nearby cropland source of leached nitrogen and where trees extend their roots below that zone [N3-F2]. The direct intercropping study is set in clay loam soil, indicating that soil texture can matter for root development and leaching control [N3-R5]. The preferential flow background also shows that macropores and soil structure strongly influence preferential flow, and that tree roots can create or alter those structures [N5-F4]. This implies that root distribution, soil texture, and the presence of macropores can amplify the leaching-reduction effect [N5-F4].

However, the evidence base has important limitations and exceptions. First, the meta-analytic review notes that N2O and NO emissions vary across agroforestry practices, and that NO emissions are similar to monocropping in some contexts, so nitrogen management is not universally straightforward [N3-F1]. Second, the global synthesis on soil gross N cycling notes that ecosystem N cycling patterns are highly variable and that no single general pattern can be applied broadly across terrestrial ecosystems [N3-F2]. This means that the reduction in leaching is not guaranteed everywhere; it depends on local soil type, climate, and land use. Third, the direct intercropping study is specific to eastern Canada and clay loam soil, so its results may not generalize directly to sandy, dry, or highly disturbed soils [N3-R5]. Finally, the broader evidence on preferential flow shows that high macroporosity can actually reduce the stained area ratio in tracer experiments, but it can also create faster, more localized preferential flow [N5-F4]. This means that tree roots can reduce leaching in some cases, but they may also create faster transport pathways in others, depending on soil structure and root architecture [N5-F4].

Overall, the strongest evidence is that agroforestry and tree-root systems reduce subsoil nitrogen leaching, especially when trees have deep rooting and when intercropping systems are established on soils where root distribution and macropore formation can intercept leached nitrogen [N3-F1][N3-F2][N3-R5][N5-F4]. The effect is amplified by deep rooting, nearby cropland sources, and favorable soil conditions, but the evidence is still context-dependent and not universally uniform [N3-F1][N3-F2][N5-F4].

While the evidence does not directly spell out mycorrhizal associations in the excerpted material, the broader context of nitrogen cycling in agroforestry systems implies that tree-root systems can extend nutrient uptake capacity and improve soil nitrogen retention through active root function and associated soil interactions [N1-R1][N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R4]. In other words, tree roots do not simply absorb nitrogen once; they create conditions in which nitrogen is retained in the soil matrix or taken up before it can leach downward.

## 2) Agroforestry intercropping changes nitrogen cycling and the belowground environment

Agroforestry intercropping systems change nitrogen cycling by altering tree-root biomass, litter inputs, and the balance of competition and facilitation between crops and trees. The branch report states that agroforestry systems transfer organic compounds such as leaf litter, dead roots, and nodules to the soil, which enriches the belowground nitrogen pool [N2-R4]. This directly supports the idea that tree-root biomass and litter inputs increase soil nitrogen availability by adding organic nitrogen sources and creating a more nitrogen-rich belowground environment [N2-R4].

The branch report also says that belowground dynamics influence nitrogen cycling and crop productivity, with fine root nitrogen positively correlated to aboveground biomass [N2-R1]. This suggests that tree-root biomass itself contributes to nitrogen cycling by maintaining a belowground nitrogen sink and by influencing the availability of nitrogen for neighboring plants. The intercropping literature further shows that pruning tree canopies changes tree root spatial and temporal distribution, which allows annual crops to develop between the trees [N2-R2]. This pruning effect implies that tree-root distribution is not static; it can shift over time, altering the spatial organization of nitrogen availability and uptake [N2-R2].

Competition and facilitation between crops and trees alter nitrogen dynamics in several ways. The branch report notes that pruning changes root distribution and that root dynamics and belowground interactions are important in agroforestry systems [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This indicates that when trees are present, crops may compete for belowground resources, but pruning can shift the balance toward facilitation by redistributing root space and reducing direct competition [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The evidence also implies that intercropping systems create feedbacks through root biomass, litter inputs, and altered root distribution, which jointly shape nitrogen availability and cycling [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Belowground feedbacks in intercropping systems emerge through root biomass, litter inputs, and altered root distribution. The branch report says these feedbacks are important and that agroforestry systems can change how nitrogen is partitioned among crops and trees [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. In other words, the presence of trees does not simply add nitrogen; it reorganizes the soil nitrogen pool and the way crops access nitrogen, often improving retention and reducing losses [N2-R1][N2-R4].

## 3) Preferential flow and soil transport processes can either accelerate leaching or be intercepted by tree roots

The branch reports also show that soil water and nutrient transport processes are central to leaching. The evidence indicates that preferential flow is rapid movement bypassing the soil matrix, and that macropores serve as the main or sole channels for long-distance transport of water and chemical substances [N5-F4]. Another source defines preferential flow as non-equilibrium flow under various environmental conditions and emphasizes that it can promote rapid solution leaching below the root zone [N5-R2]. This means nitrogen is not evenly distributed through the soil; instead, it can move quickly through preferential pathways, especially when macropores are present [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-F4].

Tree roots can intercept or redirect preferential flow by creating root pathways and macropores. The evidence notes that biological activities, including roots and soil fauna, form macropores in farmland [N5-F4]. It also states that trees can enhance preferential flow through macropores formed by their roots and associated soil fauna [N5-F4]. At the same time, the evidence suggests that root distribution and pruning can change root spatial and temporal distribution, which can influence how water and nutrients move through the soil profile [N2-R2][N5-F4]. This implies that tree roots do not passively allow preferential flow; they actively shape it by creating the physical pathways and altering the spatial arrangement of soil structure [N5-F4].

Soil structure and root distribution reduce leaching risk by modifying preferential flow connectivity and tortuosity. The evidence highlights that macropore structure strongly correlates with preferential flow and that preferential flow is affected by the connectivity and tortuosity of macropores [N5-F4]. It also notes that high macroporosity corresponds to a lower stained area ratio in tracer experiments, meaning that preferential flow is more localized and less widespread under certain conditions [N5-F4]. In addition, root architecture and distribution influence how nitrogen is intercepted and how water moves through the soil profile [N4-R1][N4-R4]. Taken together, these findings support the conclusion that soil structure and root distribution reduce leaching risk by limiting the spread of preferential flow and by increasing the time nitrogen spends in the soil matrix before reaching deeper layers [N5-F4][N5-R1][N5-R2].

## 4) Evidence that subsoil nitrogen leaching is reduced by tree-root systems

The evidence base supports the claim that tree-root systems can reduce subsoil nitrogen leaching, but the strength of the evidence varies by study type and context. The most direct evidence comes from a meta-analytic review stating that agroforestry practices almost consistently show reductions in nitrogen loss via soil erosion, runoff, and leaching [N3-F1]. A second major review explicitly says that agroforestry systems can increase nitrate retention and mitigate the global impact of a leaky nitrogen cycle in croplands, with deep tree rooting able to catch and recycle subsoil inorganic nitrogen leached below the rooting zone of linked croplands [N3-F2]. This is the clearest evidence that subsoil nitrogen leaching is reduced by tree-root systems.

A third direct study reports that tree roots in a tree-based intercropping system established on clay loam soil decreased subsoil NO₃⁻ leaching by 227 kg N ha⁻¹ and 30 kg N ha⁻¹ over two consecutive years [N3-R5]. Taken together, these sources show that reduced subsoil nitrogen leaching is not just a theoretical possibility but a documented pattern under trees and tree-rooted systems [N3-F1][N3-F2][N3-R5].

The evidence also suggests that the effect is amplified under certain environmental and management conditions. The review on agroforestry notes that N loss reductions occur through soil erosion, runoff, and leaching, implying that the reduction is most visible when water and nutrient transport pathways are altered [N3-F1]. The subsoil nitrogen review emphasizes that deep tree rooting can catch nitrogen leached below the rooting zone of linked croplands, which suggests that the benefit is especially strong where there is a nearby cropland source of leached nitrogen and where trees extend their roots below that zone [N3-F2]. The direct intercropping study is set in clay loam soil, indicating that soil texture can matter for root development and leaching control [N3-R5]. The preferential flow background also shows that macropores and soil structure strongly influence preferential flow, and that tree roots can create or alter those structures [N5-F4]. This implies that root distribution, soil texture, and the presence of macropores can amplify the leaching-reduction effect [N5-F4].

However, the evidence base has important limitations and exceptions. First, the meta-analytic review notes that N₂O and NO emissions vary across agroforestry practices, and that NO emissions are similar to monocropping in some contexts, so nitrogen management is not universally straightforward [N3-F1]. Second, the global synthesis on soil gross N cycling notes that ecosystem N cycling patterns are highly variable and that no single general pattern can be applied broadly across terrestrial ecosystems [N3-F2]. This means that the reduction in leaching is not guaranteed everywhere; it depends on local soil type, climate, and land use. Third, the direct intercropping study is specific to eastern Canada and clay loam soil, so its results may not generalize directly to sandy, dry, or highly disturbed soils [N3-R5]. Finally, the broader evidence on preferential flow shows that high macroporosity can reduce the stained area ratio in tracer experiments, but it can also create faster, more localized preferential flow [N5-F4]. This means that tree roots can reduce leaching in some cases, but they may also create faster transport pathways in others, depending on soil structure and root architecture [N5-F4].

---

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Nitrogen uptake by tree roots in agroforestry intercropping systems helps reduce subsoil nitrogen leaching through several mechanisms:

- **Direct uptake**: Tree roots absorb nitrate, ammonium, and organic nitrogen sources, reducing the amount available to leach [N1-R3][N1-R4].
- **Interception and retention**: Deeper root systems and root architecture allow tree roots to intercept nitrogen in the subsoil, while active root activity and belowground interactions enhance nitrogen retention [N4-R1][N4-R4][N2-R1][N2-R4].
- **Belowground environment change**: Tree-root biomass and litter inputs enrich the soil nitrogen pool, while pruning and root distribution alter competition and facilitation between crops and trees, creating feedbacks that improve nitrogen cycling [N2-R4][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].
- **Interception of preferential flow**: Tree roots can create macropores and alter root distribution, which intercepts or redirects preferential flow and reduces leaching risk [N5-F4][N2-R2].
- **Soil structure and connectivity**: Soil structure and root distribution reduce leaching risk by modifying preferential flow connectivity and tortuosity [N5-F4].

At the same time, the evidence is context-dependent. The most direct studies and reviews show reduced subsoil nitrogen leaching under agroforestry and tree-root systems [N3-F1][N3-F2][N3-R5], but the effect is amplified by deep rooting, nearby cropland sources, and favorable soil conditions, while exceptions exist in sandy, dry, or highly disturbed soils and in systems where preferential flow may create faster transport pathways [N3-F1][N3-F2][N5-F4].

In short, agroforestry intercropping reduces subsoil nitrogen leaching because tree roots do more than just grow downward—they actively capture nitrogen, reshape the soil environment, and intercept preferential flow pathways, all of which make nitrogen less available to leach into deeper layers [N1-R3][N1-R4][N2-R4][N4-R1][N5-F4].
